expectedText:
ADVANCE HEALTH CARE DIRECTIVE
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Lee

DECLARATION AND APPOINTMENT OF AGENT
I, Jordan Alex Lee, being an adult of sound mind, make this Advance Health Care Directive to make known my wishes regarding my own health care and to designate an agent to make health care decisions for me as described in this document. I revoke any prior advance health care directive or power of attorney for health care I have made. I designate Morgan Lee as my agent to make health care decisions for me. If Morgan Lee is unable, unwilling, or not reasonably available to act, I designate Casey Lee as my alternate agent.

THE TWO KINDS OF HEALTH CARE DIRECTIVE
California law recognizes two distinct components of an advance health care directive, and a single document can contain either or both: an individual health care instruction — Jordan Alex Lee's own direct instructions about care — and a power of attorney for health care, which names Morgan Lee as agent to make health care decisions for Jordan Alex Lee. A power of attorney for health care may also include individual health care instructions within the same document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "“Advance health care directive” or “advance directive” means either an individual health care instruction or a power of attorney for health care."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4605 (California Legislative Information text), definition of advance health care directive as either component (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4605.)
  "An adult having capacity may execute a power of attorney for health care, as provided in Article 2 (commencing with Section 4680). The power of attorney for health care may authorize the agent to make health care decisions and may also include individual health care instructions."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4671(a) (California Legislative Information text), a power of attorney for health care may also include individual instructions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4671.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual statutory structure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive.

HOW THIS DIRECTIVE MUST BE SIGNED
For this power of attorney for health care to be legally sufficient, it must state the date it is executed, be signed by Jordan Alex Lee (or by another adult in Jordan Alex Lee's presence and at Jordan Alex Lee's direction), and be either acknowledged before a notary public or signed by at least two qualified witnesses. Only one of those two methods — witnesses or notarization — is required, not both.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A written advance health care directive is legally sufficient if all of the following requirements are satisfied: (1) The advance directive contains the date of its execution. (2) The advance directive is signed either by the patient or in the patient’s name by another adult in the patient’s presence and at the patient’s direction. (3) The advance directive is either acknowledged before a notary public or signed by at least two witnesses who satisfy the requirements of Sections 4674 and 4675."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4673(a) (California Legislative Information text), legal sufficiency requirements for a written directive (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4673.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual execution requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 4673(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

WHO CANNOT SERVE AS A WITNESS
If this directive is signed by witnesses rather than notarized, the witnesses must be adults, and none of the following may act as a witness: Jordan Alex Lee's health care provider or an employee of that provider, the operator or an employee of a community care facility, the operator or an employee of a residential care facility for the elderly, or Morgan Lee (or any other individual named as agent). Separately, at least one of the two witnesses must be a person who is neither related to Jordan Alex Lee by blood, marriage, or adoption, nor entitled to any part of Jordan Alex Lee's estate on death under an existing will or by operation of law — that disinterested-witness requirement applies to only one of the two witnesses, not both.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The witnesses shall be adults."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4674(a) (California Legislative Information text), the adult-witness requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4674.)
  "None of the following persons may act as a witness: (1) The patient’s health care provider or an employee of the patient’s health care provider. (2) The operator or an employee of a community care facility. (3) The operator or an employee of a residential care facility for the elderly. (4) The agent, where the advance directive is a power of attorney for health care."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4674(c) (California Legislative Information text), categorical witness disqualifications (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4674.)
  "At least one of the witnesses shall be an individual who is neither related to the patient by blood, marriage, or adoption, nor entitled to any portion of the patient’s estate upon the patient’s death under a will existing when the advance directive is executed or by operation of law then existing."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4674(e) (California Legislative Information text), the one-of-two disinterested-witness rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4674.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual disqualification rules — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 4674) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

EXTRA WITNESS RULE FOR SKILLED NURSING FACILITY PATIENTS
If Jordan Alex Lee is a patient in a skilled nursing facility at the time this directive is signed, it is not effective unless a patient advocate or ombudsman designated by the California Department of Aging also signs it as a witness — either as one of the two witnesses or in addition to notarization.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "If an individual is a patient in a skilled nursing facility when a written advance health care directive is executed, the advance directive is not effective unless a patient advocate or ombudsman, as may be designated by the Department of Aging for this purpose pursuant to any other applicable provision of law, signs the advance directive as a witness, either as one of two witnesses or in addition to notarization."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4675(a) (California Legislative Information text), patient advocate/ombudsman witness requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4675.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of an additional, real safeguard that applies specifically to skilled nursing facility patients — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 4675(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

WHEN THE AGENT'S AUTHORITY TAKES EFFECT
Unless this directive itself says otherwise, Morgan Lee's authority to make health care decisions for Jordan Alex Lee becomes effective only once a determination is made that Jordan Alex Lee lacks the capacity to make their own health care decisions, and that authority ends if Jordan Alex Lee is later determined to have recovered capacity. Unless the directive specifies otherwise, that determination is made by Jordan Alex Lee's primary physician.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Unless otherwise provided in a power of attorney for health care, the authority of an agent becomes effective only on a determination that the principal lacks capacity, and ceases to be effective on a determination that the principal has recovered capacity."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4682 (California Legislative Information text), default trigger for the agent's authority (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4682.)
  "Unless otherwise specified in a written advance health care directive, for the purposes of this division, a determination that a patient lacks or has recovered capacity, or that another condition exists that affects an individual health care instruction or the authority of an agent or surrogate, shall be made by the primary physician."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4658 (California Legislative Information text), who makes the capacity determination (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4658.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual default timing rule and who makes the determination — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive.

HOW THE AGENT MUST DECIDE
Morgan Lee is required to make health care decisions for Jordan Alex Lee in accordance with Jordan Alex Lee's individual health care instructions, if any, and Jordan Alex Lee's other wishes to the extent Morgan Lee knows them. Where those wishes are not known, Morgan Lee must decide based on Morgan Lee's determination of Jordan Alex Lee's best interest, considering Jordan Alex Lee's personal values to the extent known.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "An agent shall make a health care decision in accordance with the principal’s individual health care instructions, if any, and other wishes to the extent known to the agent. Otherwise, the agent shall make the decision in accordance with the agent’s determination of the principal’s best interest. In determining the principal’s best interest, the agent shall consider the principal’s personal values to the extent known to the agent."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4684 (California Legislative Information text), the agent's decision-making standard (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4684.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual statutory decision-making standard imposed on a health care agent — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 4684); no additional independent source was found for this.

WHAT THE AGENT CAN AND CANNOT DECIDE
Unless this directive limits it, Morgan Lee's authority to make health care decisions for Jordan Alex Lee is as broad as Jordan Alex Lee's own authority would be — including consenting to or refusing any care, treatment, service, or procedure, and selecting or discharging health care providers and institutions. State law nonetheless withholds some decisions entirely, regardless of what this directive says: it does not authorize consent, on Jordan Alex Lee's behalf, to commitment to or placement in a mental health treatment facility, convulsive treatment, psychosurgery, sterilization, or abortion.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "An agent designated in the power of attorney may make health care decisions for the principal to the same extent the principal could make health care decisions if the principal had the capacity to do so."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4683(a) (California Legislative Information text), the breadth of the agent's default authority (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4683.)
  "This division does not authorize consent to any of the following on behalf of a patient: (a) Commitment to or placement in a mental health treatment facility. (b) Convulsive treatment (as defined in Section 5325 of the Welfare and Institutions Code). (c) Psychosurgery (as defined in Section 5325 of the Welfare and Institutions Code). (d) Sterilization. (e) Abortion."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4652 (California Legislative Information text), the statutory carve-out from any consent authority (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4652.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of both the actual breadth of a health care agent's default authority and a real, specific statutory carve-out from it — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive.

ACCESS TO MEDICAL RECORDS
Unless this directive specifies otherwise, Morgan Lee — once authorized to make health care decisions for Jordan Alex Lee — has the same right Jordan Alex Lee has to request, receive, examine, copy, and consent to the disclosure of Jordan Alex Lee's medical and other health care information. Separately, under the federal HIPAA Privacy Rule, a health care provider that is a covered entity must treat a person who has authority under state law to make health care decisions for an adult patient as that patient's personal representative for purposes of accessing the patient's protected health information.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Unless otherwise specified in an advance health care directive, a person then authorized to make health care decisions for a patient has the same rights as the patient to request, receive, examine, copy, and consent to the disclosure of medical or any other health care information."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4678 (California Legislative Information text), the authorized decision-maker's records-access right (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4678.)
  "As specified in this paragraph, a covered entity must, except as provided in paragraphs (g)(3) and (g)(5) of this section, treat a personal representative as the individual for purposes of this subchapter. (2) If under applicable law a person has authority to act on behalf of an individual who is an adult or an emancipated minor in making decisions related to health care, a covered entity must treat such person as a personal representative under this subchapter, with respect to protected health information relevant to such personal representation."
  — 45 C.F.R. § 164.502(g)(1)-(2) (eCFR text, HIPAA Privacy Rule), the federal personal-representative standard, tied to state health-care-decision authority (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-45/subtitle-A/subchapter-C/part-164/subpart-E/section-164.502)
  Known gap: The state-law records-access right and the federal HIPAA personal-representative rule are two independent sources addressing different bodies of law: the California statute is used as real evidence of a state-law records-access right for whoever is authorized to decide — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive — while the cited HIPAA provision is a real, separately sourced federal regulation about medical-record privacy and access, not the source of an agent's authority to make health care decisions in the first place; HIPAA does not create or govern that decision-making authority.

SPECIFIC WISHES FOR END-OF-LIFE CARE
Regarding treatment intended to prolong my life: ☐ I want life-prolonging treatment withheld if I am in a permanent coma with no reasonable chance of recovery. Regarding relief from pain or discomfort: ☐ I want pain relief provided even if it may hasten my death. Additional instructions regarding my physical or mental health care: ☐ None.

HOW THIS DIRECTIVE CAN BE REVOKED
While having capacity, Jordan Alex Lee may revoke the designation of Morgan Lee as agent only by a signed writing or by personally informing the supervising health care provider — not by any other method. Any other part of this directive can be revoked at any time and in any manner that communicates an intent to revoke, without needing a signed writing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A patient having capacity may revoke the designation of an agent only by a signed writing or by personally informing the supervising health care provider."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4695(a) (California Legislative Information text), the stricter method for revoking an agent designation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4695.)
  "A patient having capacity may revoke all or part of an advance health care directive, other than the designation of an agent, at any time and in any manner that communicates an intent to revoke."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4695(b) (California Legislative Information text), the looser method for revoking everything else (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4695.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual, non-uniform revocation mechanics — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 4695) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

WHAT A LATER DIVORCE DOES TO AN AGENT DESIGNATION
If Morgan Lee is Jordan Alex Lee's spouse and, after this directive is executed, Jordan Alex Lee's marriage to Morgan Lee is dissolved or annulled, the designation of Morgan Lee as agent is automatically revoked by that dissolution or annulment alone. If Jordan Alex Lee later remarries Morgan Lee, the revoked designation is automatically revived.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "If after executing a power of attorney for health care the principal’s marriage to the agent is dissolved or annulled, the principal’s designation of the former spouse as an agent to make health care decisions for the principal is revoked."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4697(a) (California Legislative Information text), automatic revocation of a spouse-agent designation on divorce (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4697.)
  "If the agent’s authority is revoked solely by subdivision (a), it is revived by the principal’s remarriage to the agent."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4697(b) (California Legislative Information text), automatic revival on remarriage (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4697.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a real, automatic default specific to this state's Health Care Decisions Law — not an assumption that it mirrors this state's separate rule for wills, and not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 4697) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

A HEALTH CARE PROVIDER'S DUTY TO COMPLY OR TRANSFER
Except for two statutory exceptions described below, a health care provider or health care institution treating Jordan Alex Lee must comply with Jordan Alex Lee's individual health care instructions and with any health care decision made by Morgan Lee or another person then authorized to decide for Jordan Alex Lee, to the same extent as if Jordan Alex Lee had made the decision personally. A health care provider may decline for reasons of conscience, or because the instruction or decision requires medically ineffective health care or health care contrary to generally accepted health care standards; a health care institution may decline based on a conscience-based policy that was timely communicated to Jordan Alex Lee or Morgan Lee. In any of these cases, the provider or institution must promptly say so, make all reasonable efforts to transfer Jordan Alex Lee to a provider or institution willing to comply, and continue care — including pain relief and other palliative care — until the transfer happens or appears impossible.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Except as provided in Sections 4734 and 4735, a health care provider or health care institution providing care to a patient shall do the following: (a) Comply with an individual health care instruction of the patient and with a reasonable interpretation of that instruction made by a person then authorized to make health care decisions for the patient. (b) Comply with a health care decision for the patient made by a person then authorized to make health care decisions for the patient to the same extent as if the decision had been made by the patient while having capacity."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4733 (California Legislative Information text), the compliance duty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4733.)
  "A health care provider or health care institution that declines to comply with an individual health care instruction or health care decision shall do all of the following: (a) Promptly so inform the patient, if possible, and any person then authorized to make health care decisions for the patient. (b) Unless the patient or person then authorized to make health care decisions for the patient refuses assistance, immediately make all reasonable efforts to assist in the transfer of the patient to another health care provider or institution that is willing to comply with the instruction or decision. (c) Provide continuing care to the patient until a transfer can be accomplished or until it appears that a transfer cannot be accomplished. In all cases, appropriate pain relief and other palliative care shall be continued."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4736 (California Legislative Information text), the notify-and-transfer duty when a provider declines (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4736.)
  "(a) A health care provider may decline to comply with an individual health care instruction or health care decision for reasons of conscience. (b) A health care institution may decline to comply with an individual health care instruction or health care decision if the instruction or decision is contrary to a policy of the institution that is expressly based on reasons of conscience and if the policy was timely communicated to the patient or to a person then authorized to make health care decisions for the patient."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4734 (California Legislative Information text), the reasons-of-conscience exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4734.)
  "A health care provider or health care institution may decline to comply with an individual health care instruction or health care decision that requires medically ineffective health care or health care contrary to generally accepted health care standards applicable to the health care provider or institution."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4735 (California Legislative Information text), the medically-ineffective/contrary-to-standards exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4735.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual compliance duty and its real exceptions — reasons of conscience, and a separate exception for care that's medically ineffective or contrary to generally accepted health care standards — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive.

GOOD-FAITH IMMUNITY FOR PROVIDERS AND AGENTS
A health care provider or health care institution that acts in good faith, consistent with generally accepted health care standards, is not subject to civil or criminal liability or professional discipline for complying with a health care decision it believes in good faith was made by someone with authority to make it. Morgan Lee, acting as agent, is likewise not subject to civil or criminal liability or professional discipline for health care decisions made in good faith.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A health care provider or health care institution acting in good faith and in accordance with generally accepted health care standards applicable to the health care provider or institution is not subject to civil or criminal liability or to discipline for unprofessional conduct for any actions in compliance with this division, including, but not limited to, any of the following conduct: (a) Complying with a health care decision of a person that the health care provider or health care institution believes in good faith has the authority to make a health care decision for a patient, including a decision to withhold or withdraw health care."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4740 (California Legislative Information text), provider/institution good-faith immunity (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4740.)
  "A person acting as agent or surrogate under this part is not subject to civil or criminal liability or to discipline for unprofessional conduct for health care decisions made in good faith."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4741 (California Legislative Information text), agent/surrogate good-faith immunity (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4741.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual immunity and its real limit — the protection runs only to good-faith conduct, and the same statute separately imposes civil damages, and in some circumstances criminal homicide liability, on a provider, agent, or anyone else who acts in bad faith, such as by intentionally falsifying, concealing, or fraudulently inducing a directive — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive.

CALIFORNIA'S OPTIONAL STATUTORY FORM
California Probate Code provides an optional statutory form for an advance health care directive. Using that state-provided form is not required — any writing that satisfies the execution requirements described above is legally sufficient, and an individual may complete or modify all or any part of the statutory form.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The form provided in Section 4701 may, but need not, be used to create an advance health care directive. The other sections of this division govern the effect of the form or any other writing used to create an advance health care directive. An individual may complete or modify all or any part of the form in Section 4701."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4700 (California Legislative Information text), the optional statutory form (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4700.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a state-provided model form actually exists and is optional — not a recommendation about which format to use, and not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 4700); no additional independent source was found for this.

SIGNATURES
Signature of Jordan Alex Lee: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________

This directive is signed either before a notary public or in the presence of two qualified witnesses, whose acknowledgment or signatures and declarations appear on an attached page.
